questions.text: How does a request travel from Engine.ServeHTTP through the middleware/handler chain to a route's final handler, and what role does Context.Next() play in driving that flow?

goldFacts.statement: Engine.ServeHTTP calls engine.handleHTTPRequest(c) to begin routing the incoming request.
Once c.handlers has been set to the matched route's HandlersChain (gin-q1-f6), handleHTTPRequest calls c.Next() to execute it.
Context.Next()'s loop body invokes c.handlers[c.index](c) — this is the mechanism that actually runs the middleware/handler chain.

RouterGroup.combineHandlers appends a route's own handlers after the group's already-copied middleware (gin-q2-f4) via copy(mergedHandlers[len(group.Handlers):], handlers), producing the single HandlersChain that Next() (gin-q1-f3) later iterates.
handleHTTPRequest looks up the request path in the method's radix tree via root.getValue(rPath, c.params, c.skippedNodes, unescape).

When that lookup finds a match, handleHTTPRequest assigns c.handlers = value.handlers — the HandlersChain combineHandlers built at registration time (gin-q1-f4) becomes the exact chain Next() executes at request time.

questions.text: Why does middleware attached globally via Engine.Use still run on a request that hits the 404 (no matching route) fallback path, and what recomputes the fallback handler chain to include it?

goldFacts.statement: Engine.Use calls engine.RouterGroup.Use(middleware...) to append the given middleware to the engine's own accumulated Handlers list.

Engine.Use calls engine.rebuild404Handlers() immediately after appending the middleware (gin-q2-f1), so attaching global middleware after NoRoute was already configured still refreshes the 404 fallback chain.
rebuild404Handlers recomputes engine.allNoRoute as engine.combineHandlers(engine.noRoute) — combineHandlers here is the method Engine inherits from its embedded RouterGroup.

combineHandlers copies the RouterGroup's own accumulated Handlers (the global middleware list Engine.Use appends to) to the front of the merged chain via copy(mergedHandlers, group.Handlers) — this is the specific step that puts global middleware into engine.allNoRoute.

When handleHTTPRequest finds no matching route, it sets c.handlers = engine.allNoRoute — the global-middleware-plus-noRoute chain computed above (gin-q2-f3, gin-q2-f4) — immediately before the serveError call examined in gin-q2-f6.

serveError calls c.Next() — the same Next() whose loop over c.handlers (established in gin-q1-f3) executes the handler chain — which is why middleware attached globally via Use() (e.g. Logger/Recovery) still runs on a request that never matched a registered route.

questions.text: How does registering a route with RouterGroup.GET travel through RouterGroup into Engine.addRoute and the per-method radix tree, and how does Engine.Routes() read the registered routes back — including which handler in each node's stored chain it reports?

goldFacts.statement: RouterGroup.GET is a shortcut that calls group.handle(http.MethodGet, relativePath, handlers).
RouterGroup.handle calls group.engine.addRoute(httpMethod, absolutePath, handlers), handing the merged handlers and absolute path off to the Engine's route tree.
Engine.addRoute's route-registration step is calling root.addRoute(path, handlers), which inserts the new route into the per-method radix tree in engine.trees.
node.addRoute in tree.go is the function that actually inserts the path and its handlers into the radix tree used for request matching.
Engine.Routes() walks engine.trees via the iterate() helper to read back every registered method/path/handler as RouteInfo.

iterate(), the recursive helper Engine.Routes() drives, reads each route's reported Handler via root.handlers.Last() — the handler chain stored on that radix-tree node by node.addRoute/insertChild at registration time, not anything a text search on the identifier addRoute would show on its own.

   - Control returns back up the call stack, allowing middleware functions that were deferred around `Context.Next()` to run after the main handler finishes.

The routing process in Gin involves several layers, each playing a crucial role in how routes are registered and traversed. Here’s a detailed explanation:

1. Registering a Route with RouterGroup.GET:
- When you call RouterGroup.GET(path, handler), it internally calls the RouterGroup's method to register the route.
- This method delegates the registration to the parent Engine's addRoute function, passing the HTTP method, the route path, and the handler chain.
2. Passing Through RouterGroup into Engine.addRoute:
- The addRoute function in the Engine adds the route to a per-method radix tree (a specialized prefix tree optimized for routing).
- Each HTTP method (GET, POST, etc.) has its own radix tree, ensuring quick lookups for routes of a specific method.
3. Inserting into the Per-Method Radix Tree:
- The radix tree stores nodes representing segments of route paths.
- Each node can store one or more handlers in a chain (a linked list of handlers).
- When adding a route, the radix tree is traversed to find the correct position:
  - If the path segment exists, it moves down the tree.
  - If not, it creates new nodes.
- The handler chain associated with the terminal node contains the handlers for that route.
4. Reading Registered Routes with Engine.Routes():
- The Engine.Routes() method iterates through all per-method radix trees.
- It collects route information by traversing each radix tree to find all endpoints (leaf nodes).
- For each endpoint node, it retrieves:
  - The route path (constructed from the node’s position in the tree).
  - The chain of handlers stored in that node.
- It reports back the registered routes along with the associated handlers.
- Usually, it reports the entire chain of handlers stored in each node, showing the sequence of functions that will handle requests for that route.

Summary:
- The registration flows from RouterGroup.GET → Engine.addRoute → insertion into the per-method radix tree, building nodes and chains.
- The Engine.Routes() method traverses these trees to list all routes, reporting each route’s path and the entire chain of handlers stored in each terminal node.

This process ensures efficient route matching and provides introspection capabilities through the Routes() method.
